title: 9 Real-Life Instances Of Demonic Possession That Are More Horrifying Than 'The Exorcist'
excerpt: From the terrifying true cases that inspired 'The Conjuring' movies to chilling mysteries that still haunt us today.
content:
From The Real-Life ‘Conjuring’ To A Satanic Nun, Explore 9 Horrifying Tales Of Demonic Possession

Published October 22, 2026

The Demonic Possession Of Arne Cheyenne Johnson, The Accused Murderer Behind The Devil Made Me Do It

Bettmann Archive/Getty ImagesArne Cheyenne Johnson arriving at court in March 1981.

On Feb. 16, 1981, 19-year-old Arne Cheyenne Johnson stabbed 40-year-old Alan Bono to death in Brookfield, Connecticut. But though Johnson’s guilt seemed undeniable, his defenders offered a surprising explanation for his actions: They said that the murder was caused by demonic possession.

“The courts have dealt with the existence of God,” Johnson’s attorney, Martin Minella, said according to The New York Times. “Now they’re going to have to deal with the existence of the Devil.”

Indeed, Johnson’s defense team insisted that he’d been possessed by the same demon that had reportedly possessed his girlfriend’s younger brother. The 12-year-old had allegedly had visions of an old man with “burnt” skin, suffered from severe convulsions, and kicked, bitten, and cursed at his family.

Bettmann/Getty ImagesArne Cheyenne Johnson was found guilty of first-degree manslaughter and served five years in prison.

While trying to help his girlfriend’s family with the younger brother, Johnson had allegedly spoken straight to the demon. Multiple times, the family insisted, he had told the purported demon, “Come into me – leave the little lad alone.”

That appeal, they said, had caused Johnson’s demonic possession.

But though a subsequent investigation found that Johnson’s girlfriend’s family had sought help from priests — and even from paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren — for their son, local police insisted that there was nothing supernatural about Bono’s murder.

“It was not an unusual crime,” Police Chief John Anderson told The Washington Post. “Somebody got angry, an argument resulted.”

A jury seemed to agree. After deliberating for three days, they found Arne Cheyenne Johnson guilty of first-degree manslaughter. He was later sentenced to 10 to 20 years in prison, though he served five.

His story, though, has lived on. Forty years after Johnson stabbed Bono to death, the 2021 film The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It dramatized this possible case of demonic possession.

The Possession Of The ‘Annabelle’ Doll

Warren’s Occult MuseumEd and Lorraine Warren with the Annabelle doll.

Arne Cheyenne Johnson’s case of demonic possession wasn’t the first to attract the attention of Ed and Lorraine Warren. The paranormal investigators also allegedly investigated the demonic possession of Annabelle the doll.

As the story goes — largely told by the Warrens themselves and uncorroborated by others — the Annabelle doll first surfaced in 1970 when it was gifted to a young nurse named Donna, sometimes referred to as Deirdre. Donna brought the doll home where it allegedly began to exhibit odd behavior.

Not only did Donna and her roommate Angie begin to suspect that the doll could move itself around their apartment, but they also found eerie notes on parchment paper that said, “Help Me.” After the doll appeared to attack Angie’s boyfriend, the girls called in a medium, then a priest, who alerted Ed and Lorraine Warren to the possible case of demonic possession.

Warren’s Occult MuseumThe Annabelle Doll was locked in a special case to try to prevent it from causing more mayhem.

According to the Warrens, the Annabelle doll was possessed by a demon — and the demon was looking to move to a human host. “This spirit manipulated the doll and created the illusion of it being alive in order to get recognition,” they explained. “Truly, the spirit was not looking to stay attached to the doll, it was looking to possess a human host.”

After ordering an exorcism of Donna and Angie’s apartment, the Warrens took possession of the doll. They moved it to a specially-made glass and wood case, which they inscribed with the Lord’s Prayer and Saint Michael’s Prayer. Despite this precaution, Annabelle was still able to allegedly cause injury to anyone who laughed at her or who mocked her.

Though Ed and Lorraine Warren have since died (Ed in 2006 and Lorraine in 2019), the doll has remained in their Monroe, Connecticut museum. However — for better or for worse — the doll will be displayed at Warren’s Seekers of the Supernatural Paracon at the Mohegan Sun casino in Connecticut in 2022.
